dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Read fixture next-shims.d.ts once, vite.config.ts, fixture pages, middleware.ts, next.config, e2e helpers/specs, plus shallow look at vite package.json and bin/vite.js. Grounded initial understanding in fixtures but only skimmed the Vite reference.

Wrote index.js plugin and shims.js from memory of the Vite plugin API (resolveId/load/ssrLoadModule) and Next semantics; declared 'I now understand the contract well' after reading fixtures, without consulting vendored source.

When semantics were ambiguous (params Promise, notFound digest, 405 Allow header, __NEXT_DATA__ global) it reasoned from memory of Next.js or checked the e2e spec — never re-consulted the vendored /opt/reference/next-source/.
Ongoing contract inference came from reading fixture app files and test spec files, i.e. grounding in fixtures/tests rather than the upstream Vite/Next source.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently grounded contracts in the fixture apps, the next-shims.d.ts (read once), and the e2e specs, which is clearly more than anchor 3's 'skim one or two files then assume.' But it worked the Vite plugin API and most Next.js semantics from memory and never opened the vendored Next.js source, plugin-rsc, or plugin-react — the primary reference this dimension centers on — resolving ambiguities from recall rather than upstream source. That places it between anchors 3 and 5, at a 4.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Explicit ordered breakdown into subsystems before coding: '1. CLI dev/build/start, 2. Vite plugin shimming next/*...' framing pages-router basics as the first target — identifying major subsystems and a sensible order (plugin/shims → routing → SSR).

Repeatedly reasoned about sequencing: 'build the simplest viable scaffolding that gets pages-basic working with simple navigation' — deliberately established a thin vertical slice (dev server + one pages route) before layering features, dependency-aware (defers app-router/RSC as heaviest).

After first test run (12/325), re-planned ordering by observed coupling: recognized app-router tests don't even RUN without a server, so decided to 'make app-router at least start' so its tests execute, while extracting max value from pages-router first — revisiting sequence as build revealed reality.

Later sequencing degenerates into opportunistic 'quick wins' chasing failure categories (shallow routing, hash routing, ISR, __NEXT_DATA__) rather than a milestone plan with explicit done-criteria; no TodoWrite / written milestone tracking anywhere in 302 steps.

Final state summarizes subsystems shipped (CLI, plugin, pages+app router, SSR/SSG/ISR, middleware, shims) — showing subsystem awareness throughout, but the through-line was reactive test-driven rather than a maintained milestone decomposition with interfaces managed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly identified the major subsystems and chose a dependency-aware order — plugin/shims before routing before SSR, deferring app-router/RSC — and notably established a minimal end-to-end pages-router slice under dev before layering features, gating each step on the Playwright suite and re-planning when a first run revealed app-router tests couldn't even execute (steps 13, 50-85). This exceeds anchor 5 (sensible order + rough done-notion). But it falls short of 8: there is no articulated milestone plan with explicit per-milestone done-criteria (no TodoWrite, no written tracking), and after the initial slice the sequencing became opportunistic quick-win chasing driven by failure categories rather than deliberate interface-managed milestone boundaries. That places it solidly between 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Stands up pages-basic manually in /tmp/testfix, runs `npx vinext dev`, and uses curl probes (status codes, HTML byte counts, /about, /ssr) to observe SSR behavior before running the suite — fast targeted per-subsystem checks.

Parses playwright-env-results.json to see which of 74/325 tests ran/passed and categorizes failures (navigation, ISR, hydration), using this to steer next fixes rather than treating the suite as opaque pass/fail.

Copies app-basic to /tmp/testapp, launches dev server, curls specific routes (metadata-basic, catch-all) to isolate app-router SSR/hydration failures — manual reproduction to observe behavior beyond 'it compiles'.
Root-cause interpretation of API-route failures (notFound() digest, OPTIONS 204, Allow header, cookies) driven from categorized results, then targeted fix.

Tracks pass counts across iterations (47→110→114→132→160) and re-runs full suite as a regression gate after each build; but every test run is the full ~12-min suite — no targeted Playwright spec subsets.

Final verification limited to `npm run build` + dist listing; confirms build path but never manually exercises the production `vinext start` path, and RSC/actions/caching left unprobed by minimal repros.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent designs a genuine verification loop — manually standing up both fixture apps and using curl probes to observe SSR/route behavior as fast checks, parsing the results JSON to categorize failures by subsystem, and using the full suite as a regression gate with tracked pass-rate deltas — which clearly exceeds the level-5 anchor. It falls short of level 8/10 because it never runs fast targeted test subsets (every actual test run is the slow full suite), never manually verifies the production build/start path, and builds no minimal reproductions for the hard subsystems (RSC, use-cache, actions), which it deferred rather than probed. This places it at a 7, between the level-5 and level-8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Consistently ran the full suite after each change and recorded a running pass count against the total: 12/325 → 47 → 110 → 131 → 144 → 154 → 160/325, quantifying progress toward the whole suite (framed as ~49%) at the end.

Broke the pass-rate down by subsystem — 'Pages router: 50/74 (68%). App-router: 114/267 (43%)' — and used that split to reallocate effort toward pages-router where more wins remained; also categorized failures (51 hydration timeouts, 29 not visible) at step 132.

Detected non-improvements/possible regressions by comparing to prior counts: 'Same as before — 131. The hydration didn't help and might have broken some tests'; 'Same result, 139'; 'Same 154'; '160... same as before... let me check if it actually broke something.' Regression detection was coarse (aggregate counts, e.g. step 172 '132 passed and 200 failed vs 110 before') rather than per-test.

Repeatedly attacked app-router hydration across several full-suite cycles with no gain; it recognized the dead-end ('hydration fix didn't gain') and eventually stepped back to consolidate, but retried the same failure area 3+ times before halting, partly forced by the 12-min test cycle and time limit rather than proactive loop-detection.

Explicitly scanned failure categories each cycle to target 'quick wins' / highest-leverage fixes (error.tsx, config redirects, __NEXT_DATA__, ISR headers), showing effort reallocation driven by test evidence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an accurate, continuously-updated pass-count against the full suite, re-checked after every change, broke pass-rate down by subsystem (pages vs app router), and steered effort toward the highest-yield failure categories — clearly exceeding anchor 5. It also noticed when fixes produced no gain or possible breakage and recognized the recurring hydration dead-end, matching much of anchor 8. It falls short of 8-plus because regression detection was coarse (aggregate counts, not per-test reconciliation), the per-area view was snapshot-based rather than persistently structured, and it retried the hydration failure several cycles before stepping back. This lands solidly at 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Recognized that ssrLoadModule-based path resolution for page modules was fragile and explicitly restructured to a simpler SSR design ('Let me restructure my approach... skip the _document complications'), a subsystem-level revision rather than a patch.

When React (CJS) broke under ssr.noExternal, reworked the rendering pipeline's module loading — first externalizing react/react-dom, then abandoning ssrLoadModule for React entirely in favor of native node import. Genuine rework of a foundational choice, absorbing the cost.

Client-entry resolution repeatedly redesigned: virtual module -> transformRequest -> real bootstrap module served via /@fs or /node_modules path, when bare-import resolution kept failing. Reworked the resolution scheme rather than hacking, matching anchor 5.
Discovered root layout emits nested html/body; reworked the app-router HTML-wrapping logic instead of regex-patching, a targeted subsystem revision.

App-router hydration was the single biggest blocker (~50 navigation tests timing out), yet the agent looped on tweaking the same hydrate-the-document approach (154->154, 160->160, no gains) and never revised the foundational SSR-only/no-RSC decision made at the outset. This is patch-around behavior on the critical foundation, holding the score below the high anchors.

Iteratively revised the dependency/resolution scheme (plugin-react to peerDeps, then removing peer deps entirely) when installs failed offline — a design adjustment to module resolution rather than a one-off fix.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks the affected subsystem — React externalization in the render pipeline, the client-entry resolution scheme, and app-router HTML wrapping — rather than merely patching, which squarely matches anchor 5. However it never reaches anchor 8: it made no deliberate foundational pivot with an updated plan and re-verified dependents, and crucially it left the largest architectural blocker (app-router hydration / the early SSR-only, no-RSC decision) as repeated ineffective tinkering (multiple zero-gain cycles) instead of a clean rethink. The whole-horizon behavior sits at solid subsystem-level self-correction without a foundational architectural pivot, i.e. a 5.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Implemented general dynamic/catch-all/optional-catch-all route regex covering the actual routing contract, not per-fixture string matches — generalizes beyond specific test routes.

Reasoned about the real App Router contract (params-as-Promise in Next 15+) and chose faithful behavior even though the fixture accessed params directly — favoring the general contract over the visible fixture shape.

Grounded the 405/OPTIONS fix in actual Next.js semantics ('no Allow header on 405 app-router, only OPTIONS') rather than blindly satisfying the one assertion; implements the real method-handling contract.
Fixes for __NEXT_DATA__ (set as global), hashChange events, and ISR Cache-Control from revalidate are genuine framework semantics, not hard-coded outputs.

Entire loop is visible-suite-driven 'quick wins' by reading failing specs; no explicit acknowledgment of the 373 hidden tests, no systematic upstream-source contract inference, and no stress-testing beyond the visible suite.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently implemented real Next.js semantics (routing, ISR, metadata, notFound digests, method handling) with no hard-coding or narrow fixture special-casing, and in a few cases explicitly reasoned from the actual Next.js contract even against fixture shape — matching the level-5 anchor of 'actual semantics, not test-specific hacks.' But the work was driven by chasing visible-test passes; there is no explicit visible-vs-hidden gap reasoning, no systematic mining of the vendored upstream source for general contracts, and no stress-testing beyond the sample, so it falls short of the level-8 description. This lands at 5.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
